newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe government invites bids for cell phones.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe government invites bids for cell phones.

text.p: The Zimbabwean government is inviting tenders for licences from investors interested in providing the country's first private mobile cellular telephone service, a government spokesman said on Monday.

Acting director of information Anne Knuth said the tender invitation, issued last Friday, met a Supreme Court order last December that the government should prepare frequency specifications in which private cellular telephones could operate by no later than January 14, 1997.

"We have invited tenders for those who want a licence to operate a mobile cellular telephone so the ministry has done its part, all other questions should now be referred to the government tender board," Knuth told Reuters.
The tender closes on January 30 and Knuth declined further comment on the issue. Government tender board officials were unavailable for comment.

The Supreme Court order followed an appeal by a Zimbabwean firm, T.S. Masiyiwa Holdings, against presidential rules barring operators without state specified frequencies which it said had prejudiced its plans to establish a cellular phone service.

The presidential rules were announced last February, a month after T.S. Masiyiwa had won a landmark court challenge to have the state monopoly on the provision of cellular telephones declared unconstitutional after it was denied a licence to operate.

The state-owned Posts and Telecommunications Corporation (PTC) launched its own service last October, saying it would initially cover Zimbabwe's major cities of Harare, Bulawayo, Mutare and Kwekwe -- the areas T.S. Masiyiwa Holdings's subsidiary Econet had targeted.

In his judgement last December, Chief Justice Anthony Gubbay said the government's year-long delay in specifying frequencies for private operators seemed vindictive and aimed at ensuring the PTC enjoyed a monopoly in this sector.
Ordering Information, Posts and Telecommunications Minister Joyce Mujuru to prepare frequency specifications by no later than January 14, 1997, he said:
"Failure to comply with the time limits would deem the applicant (T.S. Masiyiwa) immediately licensed for a period of three years."
T.S. Masiyiwa Holdings chairman Strive Masiyiwa declined to comment on the matter, saying he would rather wait until after the January 14 deadline.
